uncited: Sorting Algorithms in volume rendering splatting reorder volumetric primitives (typically 3D Gaussian splats) by depth to ensure correct front-to-back alpha blending [S1, unofficial][S2, unofficial].
This solves the order-dependent transparency problem inherent in splatting, where incorrect draw order leads to visual artifacts [S1, unofficial][S2, unofficial].
Unlike siblings that may use partial ordering or hardware-specific tricks, this family focuses on generating a strict depth-sorted index buffer for the rasterizer [S1, unofficial].
The splatting family shares the fundamental mechanism of treating volumetric data as a set of geometric or parametric primitives that are transformed and rasterized [S1][S3, unofficial][S4].
**Primitive Representation:** The volume is decomposed into primitives.
These may be explicit geometric shapes (cubes, cells, splats) or implicit functions sampled via texture hardware [S1][S3, unofficial][S4].

Each primitive $k$ is defined by its position $\mathbf{p}_k$, density/extinction coefficient $g_k$ or $\rho_k$, and a reconstruction kernel $h$ (typically a Gaussian) [S1][S6, unofficial][S10, abstract only, unofficial].
**Transformation:** Primitives are transformed from volume space to screen space using the Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix or specific factorizations (e.g., shear-warp) [S2, S3, unofficial][S4].
For perspective projections, the kernel shape may be distorted (e.g., EWA splatting) to account for foreshortening [S6, unofficial][S10, abstract only, unofficial].
**Rasterization:** The transformed primitives are projected onto the 2D image plane.
This step leverages hardware-accelerated scan-conversion, depth testing, and blending [S1][S2, S3, unofficial][S4].

**Compositing:** Contributions are accumulated to form the final image.
This is typically done using alpha blending in back-to-front or front-to-back order to handle transparency correctly [S1][S2, S3, unofficial][S7].
Splatting compositing is performed along sheets (all pixels at once for a set of voxels), whereas ray-casting composites along rays (one sample at a time) [S10, abstract only, unofficial].
**Hardware Acceleration:** Most methods in this family rely on GPU rasterization pipelines for performance, enabling real-time interactivity [S1][S2, S3, unofficial].
Originating from the need to resolve order-dependent transparency in splat-based volume rendering, these algorithms evolved alongside 3D Gaussian Splatting [S1, unofficial][S2, unofficial].
Early implementations relied on CPU sorting due to GPU limitations, while modern approaches leverage GPU subgroups and merge networks for real-time global sorting [S1, unofficial].
